ours-corpus.short: Night School's tokenizer runs, computed for this film
ours-corpus.citation: media/school/tokens/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_tokens.mjs from system/school/tokens.mjs: BPE learned on the guides' corpus (3,000 generated episodes, 47,002 words) and on the first five paragraphs of Moby-Dick (716 words), measured on held-out text.
claims: Guides' corpus: 4.39 tokens per word at 0 merges (characters plus one end-of-word symbol per word; '.' and '?' count as words), 1.80 at 50 merges, 1.00 at 136 merges (vocabulary 160). The first merge is e with the end-of-word mark; the fifth makes 'the'.
Unseen 'lamplit' is cut into l, am, p, lit (end of word). Ten runs of 136 random merges leave 1.32 to 1.67 tokens per word.

English: with 400 merges learned on Moby-Dick (716 pre-tokens, 599 words split on spaces), the opening of Pride and Prejudice takes 2.14 tokens per word; 'lighthouse' is cut into li, gh, thou, se, the same at 400 and at 878 merges.
The attention model is word-level with 46 entries: 44 words and two marks ('.' and '?').
ours-corpus.n: 47,002 corpus pre-tokens (9,334 of them punctuation); 716 and 281 English pre-tokens (599 and 233 words split on spaces); 10 random-merge seeds.
ours-corpus.does_not_prove: Anything about large tokenizers; small texts chosen to show the mechanism.

sennrich2016.short: Sennrich, Haddow and Birch 2016, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
sennrich2016.citation: Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., Birch, A. (2016). Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. ACL 2016. arXiv:1508.07909.
sennrich2016.read: full text, arXiv v5: sections 1 and 3.2, Algorithm 1, Figure 1 (on arXiv August 2015; ACL 2016). The prose writes the end-of-word symbol as a middle dot; Algorithm 1 uses </w>.
claims: Byte-pair encoding for word segmentation: start from characters with an end-of-word symbol, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols within words, and add the merged symbol to the vocabulary (section 3.2, Algorithm 1).
Rare and unseen words are represented as sequences of subword units, which lets a translation model handle them.
sennrich2016.does_not_prove: That BPE is the best segmentation for every language or task.

gage1994.short: Gage 1994, A New Algorithm for Data Compression
gage1994.citation: Gage, P. (1994). A New Algorithm for Data Compression. The C Users Journal 12(2), 23-38.
gage1994.read: a reconstructed copy (abstract and section 1), DOI 10.5555/177910.177914; the volume, issue and pages are not confirmed by that copy
claims: Byte pair encoding began as compression: replace the most frequent adjacent pair of bytes with a byte that does not occur in the data, and repeat.

melville1851.citation: Melville, H. (1851). Moby-Dick; or, The Whale. Chapter 1, paragraphs 1 to 5. Project Gutenberg eBook #2701.
claims: Public-domain English text used as training text for the English BPE.

austen1813.citation: Austen, J. (1813). Pride and Prejudice. Chapter 1, paragraphs 1 to 10. Project Gutenberg eBook #1342.
claims: Public-domain English text used as held-out text.

radford2019.short: Radford and others 2019, Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2)
radford2019.citation: Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., Sutskever, I. (2019). Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI.
radford2019.read: full text, sections 2.2 and 2.3 (confirmed by the fact-check)
claims: GPT-2 applies BPE to bytes rather than Unicode code points: a base vocabulary of 256 instead of over 130,000, so any string can be encoded (section 2.2).
radford2019.does_not_prove: That byte-level BPE is better on every measure; ours compresses slightly worse than character-level BPE on the held-out page.

ours-bytes.short: UTF-8 byte counts and byte-level BPE, computed for this film
ours-bytes.citation: media/school/tokens/facts.json (bytes section): TextEncoder byte counts; character-level and byte-level BPE with 878 merges on Moby-Dick, measured on Pride and Prejudice.
claims: UTF-8: a is 1 byte, a precomposed accented e (U+00E9) 2 (an e with a combining accent is 3), a curly apostrophe 3, the seal emoji 4.
On the held-out page, character-level BPE leaves 16 unknown tokens (7 open and 7 close curly quotes, one D and one E never seen in training); byte-level BPE leaves 0.
ours-bytes.does_not_prove: That bytes are the right base for every language model.
